analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.15 an hour in two steps.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2000, placed on the Senate calendar, and never received a committee hearing or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage, which had been stuck at $5.15 an hour since 1997, to $5.65 in April 2000 and $6.15 in April 2001 — a 50-cent increase in each of two years. It would also have ended a decades-old exemption for the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, where the federal minimum wage did not apply, by phasing the islands up to the federal wage at 50 cents every six months from a starting point of $3.55. The bill was placed on the Senate calendar but never got a hearing, an amendment vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage, most of them in restaurants, retail, hotels, and other low-wage service jobs, would have gotten a raise of about 19 percent by 2001. Workers on the islands would have seen their wage rise from as low as $3.55 toward the federal floor. Working spouses and teenagers in minimum-wage households would also benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minimum-wage workers, mainly in low-wage service jobs

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 (unchanged since September 1997) to $5.65 beginning April 1, 2000, and $6.15 beginning April 1, 2001 — a combined $1.00 an hour increase.
For a full-time minimum-wage worker, the two-step increase was worth roughly $2,000 a year at the time.
Ends the federal minimum wage exemption for the Northern Mariana Islands, phasing the islands' wage up from $3.55 by 50 cents every six months until it matches the federal minimum.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail stores, hotels, and small businesses with low-wage payrolls — would bear the higher wage cost, either through lower profits or higher prices. Northern Mariana Islands garment manufacturers and other island employers, whose exemption from the federal wage floor had made their labor costs far below the U.S. mainland's, would face a multi-year phase-up to the federal wage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers, restaurants, retail, and island garment makers

drawbacks.text: The first increase would have taken effect April 1, 2000 — days after the bill was introduced — leaving employers almost no lead time to adjust pay, schedules, or prices.

Opponents of minimum wage increases argue that a higher wage floor raises costs for small businesses and can price some entry-level or marginal jobs out of existence; the bill contained no tax breaks or small-business offsets, unlike the competing Republican proposal that year.

The Northern Mariana Islands phase-in, though gradual, would have raised labor costs in an island economy heavily dependent on garment manufacturing, an industry that had located there in large part because of the wage exemption.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A $1.00 an hour raise phased over a year was a modest, predictable increase by the standards of past minimum wage hikes, and the main cost — somewhat higher prices and payroll costs concentrated in low-wage industries — was spread thinly across consumers and businesses. The sharpest objections were the near-immediate effective date for the first increase and the harder adjustment for the Northern Mariana Islands economy. On the whole, the benefits to roughly ten million low-wage workers outweighed those transition costs, which is why similar increases were enacted in later years.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but no committee took it up, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Daschle introduced the bill on March 23, 2000, joined by nine Democratic cosponsors, including Senator Kennedy.
It was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 472 — a queue of bills awaiting Senate action.
No further action of any kind followed: no committee referral activity, no debate, no vote. The bill sat on the calendar until the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers — restaurant, retail, and hotel chains and the garment manufacturers of the Northern Mariana Islands — were better off because the wage stayed at $5.15 and the island exemption survived for the time being. Minimum-wage workers went another seven years without a federal raise, until 2007.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Minimum-wage employers, including island garment makers

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.role: Senate Democratic Leader and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 23, 2000 and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 8 Democratic senators including Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Kennedy, Akaka, Boxer, Durbin, Sarbanes, Wellstone, Reed, Mikulski).

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Controlled the Senate floor schedule in 2000
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for debate or a vote; leadership insisted on combining any wage increase with tax breaks and other business provisions, and the two sides never agreed on a package before Congress adjourned.

against.name: Low-wage employers and the Northern Mariana Islands garment industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed an increase and supported the competing package that paired a smaller wage rise with tax and labor-law concessions; the garment industry lobbied to preserve its exemption from the federal wage floor.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and Senate Republican leaders controlled whether the bill ever reached the floor.

industries.note: Fast food and table-service restaurants employ a large share of minimum-wage workers, so a $1.00 increase would have raised their payrolls directly. Their interest in keeping the wage at $5.15 ran against the raise their workers sought.
Retail chains and hotels with large low-wage staffs would have absorbed higher wage costs through margins or prices.
The garment industry had located on the islands largely because federal wage law did not apply there; the bill would have ended that cost advantage with a multi-year phase-up to the federal minimum.
